facts.statement: The genus Dromornis was described by Richard Owen in 1872.
facts.quote: authority: Owen, 1872

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Dromornis is Dromornis australis.
facts.quote: type_species: Dromornis australis

facts.statement: Dromornis species lived in Australia from the Oligocene to the Pliocene epochs.
facts.quote: Dromornis is a genus of large prehistoric birds native to Australia during the Oligocene to Pliocene epochs.

facts.statement: Dromornis species were flightless birds with greatly reduced wings and large legs, resembling modern ostriches or emus.
facts.quote: The species were flightless, possessing greatly reduced wing structures but with large legs, similar to the modern ostrich or emu.

facts.statement: Dromornis species were likely predominantly or exclusively herbivorous browsers.
facts.quote: They were likely to have been predominantly, if not exclusively, herbivorous browsers.

facts.statement: Dromornis belongs to the family Dromornithidae, which includes extinct flightless birds known as mihirungs.
facts.quote: They belong to the family Dromornithidae, extinct flightless birds known as mihirungs.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Dromornis australis was a femur found in a 55-meter well at Peak Downs, Queensland, and described by Owen in 1872.
facts.quote: The type specimen, another femur, was found in a 55 m well at Peak Downs, Queensland, and subsequently described by Owen in 1872.

facts.statement: The name Dromornis is derived from Ancient Greek words meaning 'course' or 'race' and 'bird'.
facts.quote: The name of the genus is derived from Ancient Greek, δρόμος (drómos), meaning a course, a race, and ὄρνις (órnis), a bird.

facts.statement: The term 'mihirung paringmal' is an Aboriginal word from the Tjapwuring people meaning 'giant bird'.
facts.quote: 'Mihirung paringmal' is an Aboriginal term from the Tjapwuring people of Western Victoria and it means 'giant bird'.

facts.statement: Although resembling giant emus, Dromornis is more closely related to early waterfowl of the Anseriformes order or a basal galliform.
facts.quote: Although they looked like giant emus, Dromornis and its relatives are more closely related to the earliest waterfowl of the Anseriformes order or a basal galliform.

facts.statement: Eggs of Dromornis are estimated to be 30–34 cm long, 24–29 cm wide, and weigh 12.6–14.7 kg, making them among the largest known bird eggs.
facts.quote: Eggs assigned to this genus are estimated at 30–34 cm in length and 24–29 cm in width, with an estimated mass of 12.6–14.7 kg which would be one of the largest known bird eggs.

facts.statement: The mass of Dromornis australis is estimated to range from 133 to 208 kg.
facts.quote: Mass estimates range from 133 to 208 kg.

facts.statement: Fossils of Dromornis australis are found in Pliocene deposits in Australia.
facts.quote: Dromornis australis fossils are found in Pliocene deposits of Australia.

facts.statement: A large femur fossil was discovered at Peak Downs, Queensland, at a depth of about 55 meters in a well shaft.
facts.quote: The fossil remains of a large femur were discovered at Peak Downs in Queensland, at a depth of around 55 m in a well shaft.

facts.statement: The species Dromornis australis is known from a right femur approximately twelve inches long found at Peak Downs.
facts.quote: The species is known by the right femur, around twelve inches long, obtained at the Peak Downs site.

facts.statement: Dromornis murrayi was described in 2016 based on fossils found among the Riversleigh fauna in Queensland, Australia.
facts.quote: Dromornis murrayi was described in 2016 using specimens discovered amongst the Riversleigh fauna in Queensland, Australia.

facts.statement: Dromornis murrayi lived during the Oligocene to early Miocene and is the earliest known species of the genus.
facts.quote: The period during which it existed was the Oligocene to early Miocene, making this the earliest known species of the genus Dromornis.

facts.statement: Dromornis murrayi stood about 1.5 meters high and weighed up to 250 kg, while Dromornis stirtoni could reach up to 650 kg.
facts.quote: This species stood around 1.5 metre high and weighed up to 250 kilogram, a considerable size but smaller than its congeners; the later species Dromornis stirtoni is determined to have been up to 650 kilogram.

facts.statement: Dromornis murrayi had an exceptionally small brain, with author Trevor Worthy comparing it to a very silly chicken.
facts.quote: The skull cavity held an exceptionally small brain, the description's leading author Trevor Worthy suggesting the comparison, "I mean, if a chicken was silly, these things were very much more silly."

facts.statement: Fossils of Dromornis murrayi at the Riversleigh Hiatus site date to the early Miocene and the late Oligocene to early Miocene.
facts.quote: The fossil deposits of Dromornis murrayi at the Hiatus site of Riversleigh have been dated as early Miocene and another as late Oligocene to early Miocene.

facts.statement: The temporal range of Dromornis murrayi fossils at Riversleigh is approximately 25 to 16 million years ago.
facts.quote: The temporal range of these finds is approximately 25 to 16 mega-annum.

facts.statement: Dromornis murrayi is known only from the Riversleigh fauna in northeastern Australia.
facts.quote: The only known occurrence of this species is amongst the Riversleigh fauna, the site is located in the northeastern region of the Australian continent.

facts.statement: Dromornis planei fossils are found in the Bullock Creek fauna in the Northern Territory of Australia.
facts.quote: It is known from specimens of the Bullock Creek fauna, fossils found in the Northern Territory of Australia.

facts.statement: The habitat of Dromornis planei was a semi-arid environment with low vegetation around seasonal wetlands and rivers.
facts.quote: The site of its discovery was once semi-arid, containing low vegetation around seasonal wetlands and rivers.

facts.statement: Patricia Vickers-Rich first described Dromornis planei in 1979, initially placing it in the genus Bullockornis.
facts.quote: The species was first described by Patricia Vickers-Rich in 1979, assigning it to a new genus Bullockornis.

facts.statement: Dromornis planei had a stocky build and was as large as an ostrich or emu.
facts.quote: As large as an ostrich or emu, the species possessed a stocky build.

facts.statement: Dromornis planei had a curved, deep bill and a remarkably large head and skull.
facts.quote: Its bill was curved and deep, the overall size of the head and skull was remarkably large.

facts.statement: Dromornis planei stood approximately 2.5 meters (8 feet 2 inches) tall.
facts.quote: The species stood approximately 2.5 metres (8 ft 2 in) tall.

facts.statement: Dromornis planei may have weighed up to 250 kilograms (550 pounds).
facts.quote: It may have weighed up to 250 kg (550 lb).

facts.statement: While some researchers considered Dromornis planei carnivorous due to its large shearing beak, most currently agree it was a herbivore.
facts.quote: Features of skull, including a very large beak suited to shearing, have made some researchers consider that the bird may have been carnivorous, but most currently agree that it was a herbivore.

facts.statement: Gastroliths found with Dromornis planei suggest a herbivorous diet, though some suggestions propose it had carnivorous abilities similar to terror birds.
facts.quote: Gastroliths are found with similar species of other regions, Genyornis, Ilbandornis and near relation Dromornis stirtoni, suggesting a herbivorous diet like the other species it is found alongside, yet suggestions have published that D. planei might have the carnivorous abilities attributed to the terror birds.

facts.statement: In 2010, Nguyen and Boles suggested that Bullockornis is a species of Dromornis based on skeletal traits and phylogenetic analyses, a view supported by subsequent studies.
facts.quote: In 2010, Nguyen and Boles first suggested that Bullockornis represents another species of Dromornis on the basis of many common traits observed in the cranial and postcranial skeleton of both taxa and their close relationship strongly supported by their phylogenetic analyses. Subsequent studies also agreed upon placing this species within the genus Dromornis.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Dromornis planei is related to geese and ducks or to Galliformes, with some studies supporting the latter.
facts.quote: Some paleontologists, including Peter Murray of the Central Australian Museum, believe that Bullockornis was related to geese and ducks. This, in addition to the bird's tremendous size and earlier misclassification as a carnivore, gave rise to its colourful nickname. It may be somewhat inaccurate, however, as other studies have recovered dromornithids as more closely related to Galliformes.

facts.statement: Patricia Vickers-Rich first discovered Dromornis stirtoni in 1979 in the Alcoota Fossil Beds in the Northern Territory of Australia.
facts.quote: Patricia Vickers-Rich first discovered the remains of the bird in 1979 in the Alcoota Fossil Beds in the Northern Territory of Australia.

facts.statement: The only certain occurrence of Dromornis stirtoni is fragmentary material from the Alcoota fossil site in Central Australia.
facts.quote: Large amounts of fragmentary material found at the Alcoota fossil site in Central Australia, the type location, are the only certain occurrence of the bird.

facts.statement: Dromornis stirtoni was a large feathered bird that grew to over 3 meters in height.
facts.quote: Dromornis stirtoni was a large feathered bird which grew up over 3 m in height.

facts.statement: Dromornis belongs to the Dromornithidae family, a group of large flightless birds endemic to Australia.
facts.quote: This species is from the Dromornithidae family, which is a family of large flightless birds endemic to Australia.

facts.statement: Dromornis stirtoni was compared to Aepyornis maximus, the largest species of the Aepyornithidae family.
facts.quote: D. stirtoni was compared to Aepyornis maximus by the authors, the largest of that family.

facts.statement: The narrow, deep bill of Dromornis stirtoni made up approximately two-thirds of its skull.
facts.quote: This narrow, deep bill, made up approximately two thirds of the skull.

facts.statement: The lower mandible of Dromornis stirtoni would have been around 0.5 meters long.
facts.quote: the lower mandible would have been around 0.5 metres.

facts.statement: Dromornis stirtoni had stubby, reduced wings that deemed it flightless.
facts.quote: The large bird had "stubby", reduced wings, which ultimately deemed it flightless.

facts.statement: Dromornis stirtoni was characterized by large, hoof-like toes with convex nails instead of claws.
facts.quote: D. stirtoni was also characterised by its large, hoof-like toes, which had convex nails, rather than claws.

facts.statement: As is typical for flightless birds, Dromornis stirtoni did not have a breastbone.
facts.quote: Further typical of flightless birds, it did not have a breastbone.

facts.statement: Dromornis stirtoni is found in deposits dated to the Late Miocene and early Pliocene.
facts.quote: D. stirtoni is found amongst the depositions of the Alcoota and Ongeva Local Faunas, dated to the Late Miocene and early Pliocene.

facts.statement: The habitat of Dromornis stirtoni was open woodland in a semi-arid climate with seasonal rainfall.
facts.quote: The vegetation type of the region in that period was open woodland favouring its semi-arid climate, within which seasonal rainfall occurs.

facts.statement: Fossils and tracks of other Dromornithidae species have been found in Riversleigh, Bullocks Creek, and Pioneer.
facts.quote: Various Dromornithidae fossils have been found in Riversleigh (Queensland) and Bullocks Creek (Northern Territory), as well as tracks in Pioneer (Tasmania).

facts.statement: Dromornis stirtoni likely existed alongside other dromornithids and browsing marsupials as an apex herbivore.
facts.quote: D. stirtoni probably existed in an assemblage of fauna that included other dromornithids and browsing marsupials as the apex herbivores.

facts.statement: It is widely accepted that Dromornis stirtoni was herbivorous.
facts.quote: It is widely accepted that Dromornis stirtoni was herbivorous.

facts.statement: Despite the accepted herbivorous diet, various indicators suggest Dromornis stirtoni may have been carnivorous or omnivorous.
facts.quote: Despite this however, there are various indicators that suggest the bird may have been carnivorous or omnivorous (Murray, 2004).

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding diet, but it is widely accepted that Dromornis stirtoni was mostly herbivorous, possibly occasionally scavenging or eating smaller prey.
facts.quote: In recognition of the varying opinions, it is widely accepted that whilst the large bird may have occasionally scavenged or eaten smaller prey, they were mostly herbivorous.

facts.statement: Various factors are proposed to have contributed to the extinction of Dromornis stirtoni.
facts.quote: It is proposed that various factors may have contributed to the extinction of Dromornis stirtoni.

facts.statement: Murray and Vickers-Rich suggested Dromornis stirtoni went extinct because it was out-competed for food sources due to dietary overlap with other large animals.
facts.quote: Palaeontologists Murray and Vickers-Rich suggested that the diet may have overlapped considerably with the diets of other large birds and animals, and that the subsequent converging trophic morphology could have contributed to the large birds extinction as it was 'out-competed' of its food source.

facts.statement: Alternative arguments propose that the breeding patterns of Dromornis stirtoni may have contributed to its extinction.
facts.quote: Alternative arguments have proposed that the large birds' breeding patterns may have contributed.
